title: Before you were a thing
hookLine: was there a time when the human was nothing worth mentioning (76:1)

lines: THE WORLD GOING ON WITHOUT YOU.
A QUESTION THAT ISN'T A QUESTION.
cards: Find a photo from before you were born. Your parents' wedding, maybe, or a family picnic. Everyone's laughing, squinting into the sun.
The world is going on, full of people and plans and weather. And you're nowhere. Not hiding, not waiting offstage.

Just not yet. Nobody in the picture is thinking of you, because there is no you yet to think of. Surah seventy-six opens by asking us to think about that on purpose, with a question that isn't really a question.

teach.b: Verse one, in Pickthall's translation: "Hath there come upon man (ever) any period of time in which he was a thing unremembered?"
The Arabic phrase at the end is shay'an madhkura: a thing mentioned, a thing worth speaking of. There was a stretch of time, the verse says, when the human wasn't even that.
Not a name, not a memory, not a thought in anyone's head.

teach.h: A QUESTION THAT IS A STATEMENT.
teach.b: Some commentators point out that the opening word, hal, usually a question, works here more like a statement: indeed, there came such a time. The answer is built into the asking.

teach.h: FROM A DROP TO HEARING, SEEING.
teach.b: Then verse two moves fast: We created the human from a drop, mingled, to test him, and We made him hearing, seeing. From nothing worth mentioning, to a drop, to a listener and a watcher.
Verse three: We showed him the way, whether he is grateful or ungrateful. The surah has a second name, ad-Dahr, Time, after this first verse. And it has a special place in the week.
According to hadith in Bukhari and Muslim, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ would recite it, along with surah as-Sajdah, in the dawn prayer on Fridays, and some mosques keep that custom.
There, Friday begins by remembering the human was once nothing. Why start there?
Because if you were once not even a thing mentioned, then everything since, your breath, your name, the people in your life, the very ability to hear these words, arrived as a gift.

how: Surah al-Insan (also called ad-Dahr) is recited in some mosques in the dawn prayer on Fridays, alongside as-Sajdah, following the Prophet's practice reported in Bukhari and Muslim.

games.q: the surah asks: was there a time when the human was nothing worth mentioning? what's the answer the verse builds in?
games.why: the question is really a statement: indeed there was. then a drop, then hearing and seeing: everything since is a gift.

practice: Picture the world a year before you arrived: the same sky, the same streets, maybe your parents young, and you not in it, and stay with that for a few breaths, without fear.
Then slowly add yourself back: your first breath, your name said for the first time, your eyes opening, your ears hearing. Notice each one as something that arrived.

wordCard.voice: Ad-Dahr, Time: the surah's second name, after its opening question about a stretch when the human wasn't even a thing worth mentioning. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: once, nothing. Your hands, your hearing, the people near you: none of it was always there. Day six hundred fifty-nine.
